abstract: This Fortune article examines the debate over AI's impact on labor markets, reporting that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledges both 'AI washing'—where companies falsely attribute layoffs to AI—and genuine job displacement from AI technology. The article presents conflicting evidence: a National Bureau of Economic Research study found 90% of surveyed C-suite executives reported no AI employment impact over three years, while other analysts and recent data suggest early signs of AI-driven labor market changes, particularly affecting early-career white-collar workers.
keyFindings: Nearly 90% of surveyed C-suite executives across the U.S., U.K., Germany, and Australia reported AI had no impact on workplace employment over the three years following ChatGPT's release in late 2022.

A Yale Budget Lab analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data found no significant differences in occupational mix changes or unemployment duration for AI-exposed jobs from ChatGPT's release through November 2025.

A Stanford study by Erik Brynjolfsson revealed a 13% relative decline in employment for early-career employees in jobs with high AI exposure, while experienced workers saw stable or growing employment.
Around 40% of employers expect to reduce staff as a result of AI according to the 2025 World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report.

U.S. productivity jumped 2.7% year-over-year last year, attributed partly to AI benefits, while job growth decoupled from GDP growth with only 181,000 job gains despite 3.7% fourth-quarter GDP growth.
methodology: This is a journalistic analysis synthesizing multiple studies and expert perspectives. Primary sources cited include: (1) a National Bureau of Economic Research study surveying C-suite executives across four countries; (2) Yale Budget Lab analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey data (ChatGPT release through November 2025); (3) Erik Brynjolfsson's Stanford study on early-career employment in AI-exposed jobs; (4) the 2025 World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report; and (5) commentary and analysis from various economists and tech leaders. Specific sample sizes and methodologies for most studies are not detailed in the article.
qualifiers: The article notes the data tells a 'muddied, inconclusive story' about AI's labor market impact. Martha Gimbel states 'at this exact moment, it just doesn't seem like there's major macroeconomic effects here.' The article presents conflicting evidence and acknowledges that AI's impact may follow a 'J-curve' pattern with delayed effects. Brynjolfsson's analysis suggests the market may be 'transitioning out of this investment phase into a harvest phase,' indicating that measured impacts may emerge later. The article notes this pattern 'rhymes with the 1980s IT boom' where impacts also took time to materialize.
